title: "Principal Component Analysis (PCA)"
description: "A linear method that projects data onto directions capturing the greatest variance."
term: "Principal Component Analysis (PCA)"
letter: "P"

difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Principal component analysis (PCA) finds new axes that summarize variation
in a dataset. Keeping only the most informative axes can make data easier to
visualize or reduce the number of features used by a later model.

## Technical explanation

For centered data, PCA finds orthogonal directions that maximize projected
variance. These directions are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or
equivalently right singular vectors of the data matrix. Projecting onto the
first $k$ components gives a rank-$k$ linear approximation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

PCA is useful for exploratory visualization, compression, and reducing
redundant features. It is a linear transformation, so it may not preserve
nonlinear structure; fitting it on all data before evaluation can also leak
information from held-out examples.

## How it works

Features are centered and, when appropriate, scaled. A singular value
decomposition or eigendecomposition yields components ordered by explained
variance. The chosen components transform new observations using the same
training-set centering, scaling, and projection.

## Practical example

An engineer can standardize measurements, fit PCA on the training partition,
and project both training and validation rows onto the first two components
for visualization. The preprocessing is fitted only on training data to
avoid leakage.

## Common misconceptions

- High explained variance does not necessarily mean a component is
  predictive of the target.
- PCA does not select original features; its components are combinations of
  them.
